extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, poets, and literary critics interested in poetic theory and style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging or composing poetry: style, diction, imagination, temperament, and the relation of rules to ends in poetic art. Emphasizes historical/contextual awareness and specific qualities (rhythm, condensation of thought, originality) that distinguish genius from manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of passion and passionate flow
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our faulty elder poets sacrificed the passion and passionate flow of poetry to the subtleties of intellect and to the starts of wit; the moderns to the glare and glitter of a perpetual, yet broken and heterogeneous imagery... The one sacrificed the heart to the head; the other both heart and head to point and drapery."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should preserve passionate flow and feeling rather than subordinating emotion to mere intellectual subtlety, point, or ornamental drapery. Avoid prioritizing wit or decorative effects over the emotional life of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heterogeneous, broken imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: "the moderns to the glare and glitter of a perpetual, yet broken and heterogeneous imagery..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sustained, elevated, and coherent imagery; avoid a continual parade of flashy, disconnected images that produce glitter without organic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural thought expressed in natural diction
rubrics_metrics.description: "combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the first who reconciled the heart with the head."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that fits the thought—simple, sincere diction that conveys natural feelings and ideas. Chaste and manly diction is praised when it accompanies genuine imaginative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid florid or laborious diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge admits he once "adopted a laborious and florid diction" which he deemed of "very inferior worth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florid, swelling, or overly elaborate language is inferior to natural expression; such diction is often a remnant of affectation and should be reformed in favor of clarity and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: "low creeping language and thoughts, — under the pretence of simplicity"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake mere triteness, banality, or 'low creeping' phrasing for true simplicity. Genuine simplicity is expressive and natural; affected simplicity is a vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doleful egotism and recurring favorite phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: "to excite a good-natured laugh at the spirit of doleful egotism, and at the recurrence of favorite phrases, with the double defect of being at once trite and licentious."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from self-indulgent, morbid egotism and the repetitive use of catchphrases that render verse trite and lax in taste; these are faults likely to provoke derision rather than admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile heart and head (emotion and intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the one who reconciled the heart with the head."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poetry integrates feeling and thought—emotion should be informed by intelligence, and intellect by feeling. Neither heart nor head should dominate to the exclusion of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate according to ends: rules are means to an end
rubrics_metrics.description: "Critics are too apt to forget, that rules are but means to an end; consequently, where the ends are different, the rules must be likewise so. We must have ascertained what the end is, before we can determine what the rules ought to be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the purpose or end of a poem before applying critical rules. Do not rigidly apply one set of rules to works that aim at different effects or purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical and contemporary stylistic norms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reader must make himself acquainted with the general style of composition that was at that time deemed poetry, in order to understand and account for the effect produced..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or interpreting a poem, account for the period's prevailing styles and conventions; apparent faults or virtues may be contingent on contemporary norms and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and power of combining ideas (imaginative combinatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: "where the ideas are vivid, and there exists an endless power of combining and modifying them, the feelings and affections blend more easily and intimately with these ideal creations than with the objects of the senses..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the poet's imaginative energy: vividness of concept and ability to combine and modify ideas is a mark of genius and enables the poem to affect readers through thought as well as sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and self-possession as signs of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The men of the greatest genius...appear to have been of calm and tranquil temper... In the inward assurance of permanent fame, they seem to have been either indifferent or resigned with regard to immediate reputation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate irritability or fanatical comportment with poetic genius; historically, great poets often display calmness, self-possession, and a patient temper toward reputation and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer collective meaning/coherence over isolated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of readers who "receive pleasure from the separate images and phrases successively, without asking themselves whether the collective meaning was sense or nonsense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poem's images and phrases cohere into a meaningful whole; admiration of isolated picturesque lines is insufficient if the collective meaning is incoherent or nonsensical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials in a budding great poet: fertility, condensation, rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: "Characterized by boundless fertility, and labored condensation of thought with perfection of sweetness in rhythm and metre. These are essentials in the budding of a great poet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for abundant creative imagination, concentrated/condensed thought, and refined rhythmic/metered sweetness as indicators of emergent poetic greatness. Over time habit may produce ease, but these essentials remain foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise choice and position of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge praises "the almost faultless position and choice of words" in Pope's originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate line-level craftsmanship: word choice and their placement within a line or sentence are crucial to poetic effect and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manufactured, mechanized literature that spares thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "language, mechanized as it were into a barrel-organ, supplies at once both instrument and tune...it spares the reader the trouble of thinking; prevents vacancy, while it indulges indolence...Hence of all trades, literature at present demands the least talent...the manufacturing of poems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware poems that mechanically reproduce familiar images and epigrammatic cadences to please without engaging the reader's intellect; value works that demand and reward thoughtful engagement rather than formulaic consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus imitation and the effect of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is peculiar to original genius to become less and less striking, in proportion to its success in improving the taste and judgment of its contemporaries."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that an original poet's distinctiveness may be assimilated by contemporaries, reducing apparent novelty; evaluation should distinguish original imaginative power from later imitative popularity.
